query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr has 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but its poor oxygen resistance limits practical high-temperature use. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing the alloy’s useful mechanical performance? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention and mechanism, the predicted change relative to untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr, the relevant temperature, atmosphere, exposure time, and mechanical-loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding approximately 4 atomic percent of chromium to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will promote the formation of a protective Cr2O3 surface scale during prolonged high‐temperature exposure, thereby overcoming poor oxygen resistance without sacrificing its useful mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr with a body‐centered cubic (BCC) microstructure that exhibits 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength between 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C.
generation.intervention: Alloying modification: introduce ~4 at% Cr into the base alloy during the melting/casting process.
generation.conditions: Samples are to be exposed at 1000 °C in an oxidizing atmosphere (ambient air) for an extended duration (e.g., 100 hours) under strain rates in the range of 10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent Cr2O3 protective scale on the surface along with possible minor reticulated Laves phase precipitates in the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: Chromium, being more reactive with oxygen, will preferentially oxidize to form a slow-growing Cr2O3 layer on the alloy surface. This protective film reduces further oxygen ingress and oxidation of the underlying material while preserving the alloy’s intrinsic BCC matrix and its mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Cr-alloyed HfNbTaTiZr is expected to show a significantly lower rate of oxygen uptake and thinner, more adherent oxide scales at 1000 °C, with mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) maintained or slightly enhanced relative to the untreated cast alloy.
generation.baseline: The untreated cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, with poor oxygen resistance resulting in degradation at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: The intervention is limited to around 4 at% Cr addition; deviations in Cr content might alter phase formation and mechanical behavior. The predicted benefits are specific to high-temperature (≈1000 °C) exposure in air for durations on the order of 100 hours and at strain rates between 10⁻⁴ and 10⁻² s⁻¹.
generation.uncertainty: While Cr addition has been shown to improve mechanical performance in related refractory HEAs, the exact Cr content needed and the long-term cyclic oxidation behavior under realistic service conditions require further optimization and testing.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr (control) and another set alloyed with ~4 at% Cr. Expose both sets to 1000 °C in air for 100 hours under controlled strain rate conditions (10⁻⁴–10⁻² s⁻¹). Post-exposure, perform a detailed microstructural and mechanical evaluation.
measurements: Weight gain measurements to quantify oxygen uptake
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) to analyze oxide scale morphology and phase constituents
Tensile testing at high temperature to assess yield strength and ductility
Comparison of oxide scale thickness and adhesion between treated and untreated samples
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Cr-added samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in oxygen uptake and oxide scale thickness, or if the high-temperature mechanical properties (yield strength and ductility) deteriorate compared to the untreated alloy, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract Concurrent strength–ductility improvement of HfMoTaTiZr is achieved via Cr addition and the underlying strengthening mechanism was discussed. 4.2 at% Cr addition into HfMoTaTiZr led to the formation of a Laves phase, in addition to the BCC phase. The hardness of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 is 535.8 Hv 0.3 , 56.96% higher than the reference alloy HfMoTaTiZr. The yield strength and fracture strain of HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 reach 1750.6 ± 80.3 MPa and 14.0 ± 2.9%, respectively, 207.5 MPa and 20.6% higher than HfMoTaTiZr. Solid solution hardening and the presence of the intermetallic Laves phase are believed to be responsible for the enhancement in strength and the formation of a reticulated structure of the Laves phase in HfMoTaTiZrCr 0.5 results in the improvement in ductility.

In the last few decades, the development of nickel-based superalloys has allowed a steady increase in operating temperatures of jet turbine engines, which leads to enhanced engine performance and efficiency. However, nowadays the engine operating temperatures have reached around 80% of the melting points of the materials, [1] i.e. , almost reaching the upper limit of usability, making it impossible to further increase the operating temperature. Thus, it is urgently needed to develop new materials that can withstand higher operating temperatures to achieve better performance, higher engine efficiency, and lower greenhouse gas emissions.

Among various potential candidates, such as ceramics, [3] intermetallic compounds, [6] and refractory metals, refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) [8] have drawn considerable attention in the past decade because of their very encouraging properties, for instance, high melting points, superior mechanical properties at both room temperature and elevated temperatures, [13] which makes RHEAs of great interest for high-temperature application.
